lessons.title: Trace checkout across service boundaries and transactions
lessons.overview: Order owns carts, checkout and chef-specific order state while resolving customer address facts from User-Chef and current menu/kitchen facts from Catalog. The actual creation entry point is CheckoutController: POST /api/v1/checkout calls OrderService.checkout with the verified CurrentUser and CheckoutRequest. OrderController at /api/v1/orders reads existing orders; it does not create checkout. A multi-kitchen checkout becomes a parent checkout and independently progressing kitchen orders. Understand which values are current lookups, which become historical snapshots and which writes share a local transaction before changing any of these routes.

steps.label: Start at CheckoutController
steps.detail: Read the class-level /api/v1/checkout mapping and its POST method, then follow service.checkout. Record the actor source, DTO and response shape. Keep the browser, gateway and Java route paths separate; do not infer one by copying another. Use OrderController for existing-order read behavior rather than as the creation entry point.

steps.label: Trace external reads
steps.detail: Follow address validation to User-Chef and active menu/kitchen resolution to Catalog. Identify what happens if required facts are missing or the owning service is unavailable. A downstream read must not be replaced with a browser-supplied price or another user's address simply to keep checkout moving.

steps.label: Trace grouping
steps.detail: Locate how cart lines are grouped by kitchen and how parent and child identifiers are established. Use a two-kitchen synthetic cart and list the saved graph. A kitchen-specific fulfilment field may belong to each child order, because kitchens can accept and prepare independently.

steps.label: Trace snapshots
steps.detail: Inspect the pickup, drop-off, item and package facts copied at checkout and the relevant snapshot factory tests. Mark values that must remain stable after profile or menu edits. Do not reconstruct an old order using today's mutable source data when the order already owns the historical fact.

steps.label: Trace chef lifecycle
steps.detail: Follow ChefOrderController and the service behavior for acceptance, rejection and ready-for-pickup. Write allowed prior states, resulting state and actor requirements from the actual implementation and approved specification. Do not invent preparation, compensation or refund rules from an endpoint name.

steps.label: Mark side effects
steps.detail: Separate accepted local transitions from outbox/integration work such as notification, payment or delivery scheduling. Identify the durable event reference and the uncertainty window when an external call succeeds but acknowledgment is lost. A healthy controller response alone does not prove all downstream effects completed.

lessons.example: If Kitchen A and Kitchen B are in the same cart, a new fulfilment field may need to live on each chef-specific order rather than only the parent checkout. One kitchen accepting does not establish the other kitchen's progress.
lessons.lab: Trace a synthetic two-kitchen checkout from CheckoutController through OrderService and the persisted parent/child structure. Mark every external lookup, actor check, snapshot and durable side effect. Run CheckoutSnapshotFactoryTest locally and distinguish its scope from full checkout integration coverage. Have a peer explain the difference between checkout creation, existing-order reads and chef actions using the actual source files. Do not create a real payment or delivery in this exercise.
lessons.pitfall: Do not confuse the order-read controller with the checkout-creation controller, or rewrite historical orders from current Catalog/profile data.

questions.prompt: Why does checkout copy address and package facts into the order boundary?
options: To create a catalog search index
questions.explanation: Snapshots prevent later source edits from rewriting the historical order.

questions.prompt: Which controller starts the reviewed checkout creation path?
questions.explanation: POST /api/v1/checkout in CheckoutController calls OrderService.checkout; OrderController reads existing orders.

lessons.title: Add an order capability without breaking idempotency or history
lessons.overview: Order features often change a state machine, not merely a CRUD form. Define which object owns the state, which prior states permit the action, how a repeated request behaves, what historical facts must be stored and which downstream contracts are affected. Implement authoritative rules in the owning service with the appropriate transaction and durable duplicate protection. A fictional local exercise is not an approved production status, cancellation policy or refund rule. The applied Order laboratory provides a complete review worksheet and source-backed entry points.

steps.label: Choose the aggregate
steps.detail: Decide whether the feature belongs to cart, parent checkout, chef-specific order or scheduled-order state. Write an ownership statement and identify the existing controller and service methods that own that object.

steps.label: Define transition rules
steps.detail: Write allowed source states, resulting state, required actor and invalid/repeated behavior before coding. Use the approved functional specification for product decisions and identify unresolved policy explicitly.

steps.label: Persist historical facts
steps.detail: Store values that must survive later profile/catalog edits. Plan an additive migration only when persistence changes, inspect the current next unused version and prove old-row and older-code compatibility.

steps.label: Make retries safe
steps.detail: Inspect and reuse the actual command/idempotency pattern where its guarantees match the feature. Test same-command replay, changed input under one receipt and simultaneous conflicting commands. An in-memory lock alone is not cross-replica protection.

steps.label: Publish downstream effects
steps.detail: Couple the owning transition and durable side-effect intention correctly. Inspect the outbox caller and transaction, then test the send/acknowledgment gap with mocks. Do not assume that a network timeout means a provider did nothing.

steps.label: Update clients and contracts
steps.detail: Change the customer, chef or administrator UI only after the API semantics and tests are coherent. Update strict parsers and loading/denied/failed/pending states. Record exact changed files and avoid a second Node.js business implementation.

lessons.example: An approved chef-order transition must define legal prior states, actor authorization, timestamps and duplicate behavior. Adding a new enum value alone does not update persistence constraints, consumers, clients or recovery.
lessons.lab: Design a local-only order metadata or approved-style transition exercise. Produce the owner/caller map, transition table, persistence fields, idempotency rule, downstream effect contract, API response and negative tests. Identify every real source file that would change. Keep commercial rules as explicit approval dependencies and do not run the exercise against production orders.
lessons.pitfall: Do not add a status enum and assume the feature is complete; transitions, persistence, consumers, client compatibility and rollback need alignment.

questions.prompt: What is the first behavioral design artifact for a new order state?
questions.explanation: Stateful behavior needs legal transitions and actor requirements before implementation.

questions.prompt: When should a downstream side-effect intention be accepted?
options: As part of the correctly coupled durable owning transition
On every retry as a new event
questions.explanation: The domain transition and durable intention must be coupled correctly; external completion remains a separate event.

lessons.title: Validate concurrency, retries and cross-service failures
lessons.overview: Order tests must cover failure at boundaries: unavailable address lookup, changed catalog data, repeated checkout, competing chef actions, downstream notification failure and repeated payment/delivery signals. Define the expected persisted state after every case. Release validation then checks the actual routed contract and deployed version, while rollback must tolerate data written by the new code. A successful unit test is not a completed real transaction, and a real transaction is not permission to run repeated live charges while diagnosing a problem.

steps.label: Test dependency failure
steps.detail: Verify the implemented checkout failure/recovery behavior when User-Chef or Catalog facts cannot be obtained. Assert that no incoherent partial parent/child graph is accepted and that the error is not converted into fabricated data.

steps.label: Test duplicate commands
steps.detail: Repeat an equivalent synthetic command and inspect the saved order graph and side-effect identities. Assert durable counts, not only matching HTTP responses. Reused input under a conflicting receipt must follow the existing contract.

steps.label: Test concurrent transitions
steps.detail: Submit competing chef/order actions in isolated integration tests and confirm only legal state movement wins. Verify actor ownership and the actual lock/constraint behavior rather than relying solely on a mocked repository.

steps.label: Test snapshots
steps.detail: Edit synthetic source profile/catalog records after checkout and verify the existing order remains historically stable. Include two kitchens and separate pickup/drop-off facts so accidental parent/child or source-field reuse is visible.

steps.label: Smoke affected contracts
steps.detail: For a separately authorized release, validate the exact payment, notification or delivery contract affected by the change. Record source SHA, image digest, route, actor and correlation evidence. An Order health endpoint alone cannot prove transactional correctness.

steps.label: Plan compatible rollback
steps.detail: Ensure older code can safely read data written during the new release, or define an explicit alternative recovery plan. Keep additive schema and audit evidence intact. Stop on inconsistent state and reconcile original references rather than deleting records or blindly replaying external effects.

lessons.example: A nullable additive order field may be ignored by the older application during rollback. A newly required status with no old-code meaning can be incompatible, so that risk must be addressed before deployment rather than discovered during an incident.
lessons.lab: Build an expected/actual/pass-fail matrix for a two-kitchen checkout with dependency failure, duplicate submit, one chef action, a conflicting action and repeated downstream signals. Run focused snapshot tests and relevant disposable integration tests, recording all skipped coverage. Write a release packet and rollback compatibility decision. Mark real payment, real rider booking and production acceptance NOT EXECUTED unless separately authorized and observed.
lessons.pitfall: Health endpoints and matching response bodies do not prove durable correctness under duplicate or concurrent commands.

questions.prompt: Which test best validates checkout idempotency?
options: Repeat the same command and verify one durable order graph
questions.explanation: Idempotency is demonstrated by repeated equivalent inputs producing one durable effect.

questions.prompt: What must rollback consider after new orders have been written?
options: Backward readability of newly written data
questions.explanation: The previous application must remain compatible with data created by the new release.
